question: Teacher is on a Permit to Teach in Spanish, has 90 credits, no degree yet. Can they add an elementary license later?

answer.summary: Not on the Permit to Teach itself: LICN-013 bars adding license areas to a permit, and a permit requires a bachelor's degree the teacher does not appear to have. Elementary can only be added to an IPL or CPL by passing the required examinations, not through coursework, so the path depends on first obtaining a qualifying license and the degree and prior-license facts below.

claims.text: A Permit to Teach may be requested only for an applicant who holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other North Carolina professional educator license.
The teacher is described as having no degree yet, so the permit as described does not meet the bachelor's degree requirement in LICN-017 §1(a). The analyst should confirm the teacher's degree status.
A Permit to Teach is valid only until June 30 of the fiscal year for which it was requested and cannot be extended or renewed.
The Department of Public Instruction shall not add additional teaching license areas under LICN-013 §1 to a Permit to Teach.

An applicant may add a license area only to an existing initial professional license (IPL) or continuing professional license (CPL). Adding an area to an IPL requires that the applicant has already met the examination requirements for the initial license area.

Elementary Education can be added to a license only by satisfying the applicable licensure examination requirements. It cannot be added through coursework alone, so the 24-credit-hour coursework option in LICN-013 §1(b) does not apply.

The Elementary (K-6) licensure examinations are Pearson Test 890 Foundations of Reading (required score 233) and either Pearson Test 203 Mathematics Subtest or Praxis 7813 CKT Math Subtest (required score 227 or 150).

A teacher license requires completion of an educator preparation program at the Bachelor's (A-Level) or higher degree level. Applicants with only a high school diploma or associate's degree may be licensed only in Career and Technical Education, JROTC, or Safety and Driver Education, and Spanish is not among those areas.

An Initial Professional License may be requested by a PSU for an applicant who has completed all academic, field, clinical, and other requirements for a recognized NC EPP but has not satisfied the licensure examinations. The EPP recommendation is not required in that case.

The passages do not state whether 90 credit hours can substitute for a degree or how credits convert to any license requirement, so the 90 credits cannot be counted toward a degree or license from these policies.

A permit or emergency license is treated as an A-Level salary placement, so the teacher's salary level on either would not reflect the 90 credits. Experience and degree pay are addressed separately in LICN-006, which was not fully provided.

questions_for_user: Does the teacher hold a bachelor's degree, and if so from an approved educator preparation program? Without a degree, the permit and most teacher licenses are not available.
Has the teacher ever been issued any North Carolina professional educator license, including a lateral entry license? A prior NC license makes the permit ineligible.
Does the teacher currently hold an IPL or CPL, or any other teaching license? Elementary can be added only to an IPL or CPL.
Has the teacher passed the Elementary examinations (Foundations of Reading and the math test)? These are required before Elementary can be added.
Is the teacher completing an educator preparation program, and in which program and degree level?
premise_corrections: The premise that the teacher can hold a Permit to Teach in Spanish with 90 credits and no degree conflicts with LICN-017 §1(a), which requires at least a bachelor's degree for a permit.
not_covered: Whether 90 credit hours from an institution count toward a bachelor's degree or any NC license requirement.
Whether the teacher qualifies for a Spanish license through an EPP or a Residency or Emergency license, given the current facts (the passages cover those rules but the teacher's facts are not known).
Rules for adding Elementary through an EPP completion instead of examinations, if any exist beyond LICN-013 §2(a).
Pre-2026 rules for permits or add-on licenses; the passages reflect only current versions.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the key's bottom line: a permit cannot be extended or add Elementary, Elementary requires exams for an IPL or CPL, and the no-degree facts conflict with the permit requirements. It omits the emergency and residency details in key point 5, and its cited text for LICN-013 §3(a) and §2(a) is only a heading, so those claims are not well backed.

question: Teacher holds a CPL in middle grades ELA and wants to add a Spanish K-12 area. They have 18 graduate credits in Spanish. Do the credits qualify?

answer.summary: The 18 graduate Spanish credits do not qualify on their own for a K-12 Spanish add-on, because the coursework path requires 24 credit hours with a grade of C or better in each course. The teacher would need 6 more qualifying Spanish credit hours, or could instead satisfy the licensure exam requirement (Praxis 5195 or ACTFL OPI and WPT).

claims.text: A CPL holder may request to add a new license area to an existing IPL or CPL.

To add a teaching license area, the applicant must either (a) satisfy the applicable licensure examination requirements for that area, or (b) complete 24 credit hours of coursework from an institution of higher education in the license area with a grade of C or better in each course.
The coursework path requires 24 credit hours. The teacher has 18, which is 6 credit hours short of the 24 required (24 − 18 = 6), so the 18 credits alone do not meet §1(b).

Spanish (K-12) is a special subject license area, so the coursework-only route is available for it. The exclusion that bars coursework-only additions applies only to Elementary Education and Exceptional Children: General Curriculum, not Spanish.
The examination route for Spanish K-12 (license code 521) is Praxis 5195 with a required score of 168, or the ACTFL OPI and WPT with a required rating of Advanced Low.
The 18-credit figure in LICN-006 is a graduate-pay rule, not an add-on rule. It applies to graduate degree salary authorization and does not establish eligibility for adding a license area.

The policies do not say whether graduate credit counts toward the 24-hour coursework requirement differently from undergraduate credit. §1(b) refers only to coursework from an institution of higher education in the license area, so graduate credit appears to be included, but this is not stated explicitly.

questions_for_user: Were all 18 Spanish credits earned at an institution of higher education, and did the teacher earn a grade of C or better in each course?
Does the teacher plan to earn 6 more Spanish credit hours (for 24 total) or to take the Praxis 5195 or ACTFL OPI and WPT instead?
Is the teacher's existing CPL an active continuing professional license (not an IPL or other classification)?
not_covered: Whether graduate-level credit is treated differently from undergraduate credit for the 24-hour coursework requirement.
Whether the 18-credit requirement in LICN-018 or LICN-006 has any bearing on add-on eligibility (it does not appear to).

metrics.judge_rationale: The bottom line is right: the 18 credits fall 6 hours short of the 24-hour coursework route, and the exam alternative is correctly stated. The answer hedges on whether graduate credit counts, which the key treats as settled, and it omits the $60 application fee. Claim 3's 'special subject' label is not backed by the cited LICN-010 text.

question: candidate w/ 15 yrs exp in florida, cert in ESOL, wants nc license. which one?
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

answer.summary: With 15 years of licensed experience, this candidate falls outside the out-of-state initial professional license path, which is limited to fewer than three years, so the likely target is a continuing professional license under LICN-025 section 2. That depends on whether the Florida license is a clear license under each listed criterion and whether the candidate passed the required exam for the ESOL area or meets the substantially similar test. Ask the questions below before choosing.

claims.text: An out-of-state applicant with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for an initial professional license (IPL). This is the IPL route for this candidate only if they have fewer than three years of experience, which they do not.

An out-of-state applicant with more than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for a continuing professional license (CPL). With 15 years of experience, the candidate meets the experience threshold, so the CPL route under LICN-025 section 2 is the relevant one.

To qualify for a CPL under LICN-025 section 2, the applicant must meet both criterion (a), holding a clear license from another jurisdiction, and criterion (b), holding NBPTS certification or having licensure requirements substantially similar to North Carolina's.

A clear license must be in good standing, renewable by the issuing authority, not revoked or disciplined, not subject to a pending unprofessional conduct investigation in any state, and not voluntarily surrendered while under investigation. Any of these failures would disqualify the Florida license as clear.

Substantially similar means the other jurisdiction required, at minimum, completion of a recognized EPP and a passing score on an out-of-state exam. The applicant must pass the applicable exam for each license area sought.

ESOL is a special subject area (K-12) in North Carolina, with the required test being Praxis 5362 and a required score of 155. This is the North Carolina exam requirement the candidate would need to meet if the Florida exam or NBPTS route does not satisfy the requirement.
Evidence of the out-of-state exam results must be presented at initial licensure in North Carolina. An out-of-state exam result cannot be used to convert an IPL to a CPL.
A CPL based on a clear license in another jurisdiction must meet the requirements of LICN-025.
Fee for an out-of-state initial professional license opened by an individual educator is $100, compared with $70 for an in-state initial professional license.
citations: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

questions_for_user: Does the candidate hold a current Florida ESOL license (or equivalent) that is in good standing, renewable, and not revoked, disciplined, or under investigation in any state?
Did the candidate pass the Florida exam for the ESOL area, and do they have the score evidence?
Does the candidate hold NBPTS certification?
Did the candidate complete an educator preparation program recognized in Florida? What degree level did it lead to (bachelor's, master's, specialist, or doctoral)?
Does the candidate have any other license areas in Florida that they want to add to a North Carolina license?
Is the candidate currently employed in a North Carolina public school unit or applying as an individual?
not_covered: Whether Florida licensure requirements are substantially similar to North Carolina's. The policies define the test but do not compare Florida's requirements.

The Florida experience transfer for experience credit or salary purposes. LICN-006 covers experience credit for NC public school employees, but the passages do not address out-of-state experience credit.
Whether the candidate's specific Florida ESOL license corresponds to the North Carolina ESOL area.
Whether the Florida exam passing score meets the North Carolina score of 155 for ESOL.
Pre-policy rules that applied before 2026-07-01 and whether they would have produced a different result.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the key's bottom line: 15 years rules out the out-of-state IPL, the CPL route under LICN-025 §2 applies, and more facts are needed. Each claim is backed by the cited policy text, including the ESOL test and fee figures. It omits the highest-degree-level licensing rule and does not address the Beginning Teacher Support Program exclusion.

question: Applicant has an NC Initial Professional License in music, wants to add an EC area. Has 9 semester hours in EC. Eligible?
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

calculations: Semester hours still short of the 24-hour coursework threshold in LICN-013 §1(b): 24 - 9 = 15

answer.summary: Not eligible through coursework: 9 hours is 15 short of the 24-hour threshold, and EC General Curriculum cannot be added by coursework alone. Eligibility depends on whether the applicant passes the required EC licensure exam and on the EC area sought, so confirm those before advising.

claims.text: An applicant may add a new license area to an existing initial professional license (IPL) only if the applicant has met the licensure examination requirements for the initial license area.
The applicant's initial area is music. The music licensure test is Praxis 5114 with a required score of 162, so the applicant must have met that requirement before adding an EC area to the IPL.

To add a teaching area, the applicant must either (a) satisfy the applicable licensure examination requirements for that area, or (b) complete 24 credit hours of coursework from an institution of higher education in the license area with a grade of C or better in each course.

Coursework arithmetic: the coursework path requires 24 credit hours. The applicant has 9 semester hours in EC, so 24 − 9 = 15 hours are still needed. The coursework path is not met. The policy text says 'credit hours' and does not define them as equal to semester hours, so confirm that the 9 semester hours count as credit hours for this purpose.

For Exceptional Children: General Curriculum, an applicant may add the area only by satisfying the applicable licensure examination requirements and cannot add it through coursework alone. Even 24 or more hours would not qualify for that area.

For EC General Curriculum (code 88091), the policies list these exam options: Foundational Knowledge Test 5355 with a score of 145; Pearson Test 890 Foundations of Reading with a score of 233; and Pearson Test 203 Mathematics or CKT Math 7813 with a score of 227 or 150.

Outcome by scenario: If the applicant has passed the required EC exam for the area sought, and the music exam (5114 at 162) was met for the IPL, the applicant may qualify under §1(a). If the applicant has not passed the EC exam, the 9 hours do not qualify under §1(b), and for EC General Curriculum coursework alone is never sufficient under §2(b).

questions_for_user: Which EC license area does the applicant want to add (General Curriculum, Adapted Curriculum, Learning Disabled, Cross Categorical, Behaviorally/Emotionally Disabled, Visually Impaired, etc.)?
Has the applicant passed the Praxis 5114 music exam with a score of at least 162, which is required to hold the music IPL for this purpose?
Has the applicant passed the required licensure exam for the EC area being added, and if so, which test and score?

Are the 9 hours in the EC area from an institution of higher education, and did the applicant earn a grade of C or better in each course? Are these semester hours or credit hours as the policy uses that term?
Is the applicant an out-of-state applicant, and was the music IPL issued under LICN-020 §1(c) or under §2 without exam satisfaction?
not_covered: Whether the applicant has already met the music exam requirement for the existing IPL, which the policy requires before adding an area.
The specific EC exam requirements for each EC area other than the General and Adapted Curriculum rows shown in the table.
How semester hours and credit hours are treated when counting toward the 24-hour threshold; the passages do not define this.

Whether the applicant's license classification or out-of-state status changes the requirements (LICN-025 §4 applies only to out-of-state applicants who seek to add an area based on an out-of-state exam).
Fees for adding an area, which are listed in LICN-008 but were not asked about.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the key's needs_more_info verdict, correctly identifies the music exam as a threshold, and correctly finds 9 hours is 15 short of the 24-hour route. It omits that other EC areas remain open to coursework and does not flag the garbled, duplicated General Curriculum rows, but nothing it states is materially wrong. Its claim that General Curriculum coursework is never sufficient is only partly backed by the name-only citation to §2(b).

question: rl holder, 3rd yr, bs in english, never took praxis content test. what happens at end of rl?

answer.summary: At the end of the third year, the residency license converts to an IPL or CPL only if the holder meets the applicable requirements and is recommended by the EPP by June 30 of that year; otherwise the residency license expires. Because this holder has never taken the English content test (5038, required score 167), the CPL route needs the exam passed before or during year three, and the passages do not say what happens if the first-year attempt was missed.

claims.text: A residency license converts to an initial professional license (IPL) or continuing professional license (CPL) only if the applicant meets the IPL requirements in LICN-020 or the CPL requirements in LICN-024 and is recommended by the EPP that prepared the licensee.

If the applicant satisfies those requirements by June 30 of the third year of the residency license, the IPL or CPL is effective July 1 of the next fiscal year. If not, the residency license expires, and the IPL or CPL is effective on the date the requirements are satisfied.

A residency license that is not renewed for the second or third year expires. The PSU may request reinstatement only if the license was not already renewed twice and the applicant is employed by the PSU and enrolled in a recognized EPP.

Under LICN-020, an IPL may be requested for an applicant who has completed the EPP requirements but has not satisfied the licensure examination requirements, and in that case the EPP recommendation is not required.

A CPL requires holding an IPL or residency license in North Carolina, satisfying the licensure examination requirements before or during the third year of licensure, having at least three years of licensed teaching experience, and completing a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies.

Under LICN-024, if the applicant did not satisfy the exam requirements before receiving an IPL, the applicant must attempt the examinations at least once during the first year of licensure. The holder has never taken the content test, so the first-year attempt requirement may not have been met, but the passages do not state a consequence for missing it.
For English (secondary, license code 100), the required Praxis test is 5038 with a required score of 167.
To convert an IPL to a clear CPL, the required State Board exam must be taken at least once during the first year of the license and passed before or during the third year of the license.
Licenses expire on June 30 of the calendar year in which they are set to expire unless renewed, extended, or converted under SBE policy.

question: Applicant has a BS in special education from a different state, teaching EC in another state for 3 years, wants a NC EC license. Which one?
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

answer.summary: The policies do not name a single license for this applicant. The answer turns on whether the 3 years of out-of-state teaching is counted as fewer than three, more than three, or exactly three, on which EPP was completed and whether it is recognized, and on which Exceptional Children license area is sought. Confirm those facts before choosing between an initial professional license and a continuing professional license.

claims.text: A bachelor's degree is an A-level EPP completion, which qualifies an applicant for a teacher license at the bachelor's level, but a teacher license is limited to the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP.

Exceptional Children is not one license. The teacher license areas include Exceptional Children: General Curriculum, Exceptional Children: Adapted Curriculum, Learning Disabled, Cross Categorical, Severely/Profoundly Disabled, Mentally Disabled, Academically or Intellectually Gifted, Deaf and Hard of Hearing, Visually Impaired, and Behaviorally/Emotionally Disabled.
An applicant may qualify for an initial professional license (IPL) if the applicant completed an EPP based outside North Carolina. This is one of three alternative routes.
An applicant holding a clear license from another jurisdiction and having fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience there may qualify for an IPL.

An out-of-state applicant with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for an IPL, provided the applicant holds a license in the corresponding area or completed a recognized EPP, and the applicant has either passed an out-of-state exam in that area or satisfies NC exam requirements by the third year. Elementary and Special Education: General Curriculum must satisfy NC exam requirements by the end of the third year regardless.

An out-of-state applicant with more than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for a continuing professional license (CPL), if the applicant holds a clear license, and also either holds National Board certification or the other jurisdiction's requirements are substantially similar to NC's, including completion of a recognized EPP and a passing out-of-state exam in each license area sought.

At exactly three years of experience, the applicant meets neither the 'fewer than three years' condition for an IPL under LICN-025 §1(a) and LICN-020 §1(c), nor the 'more than three years' condition for a CPL under LICN-025 §2. The applicant's situation falls in this gap for those two provisions, so the applicant may still qualify under LICN-020 §1(b) based on the out-of-state EPP.

Under LICN-001 §3(d), an EPP must be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority in the state where the EPP is located. The passages do not state whether this applicant's EPP meets that requirement.

To move from an IPL to a CPL for teaching, the applicant needs at least three years of licensed teaching experience, must satisfy the licensure exam requirements before or during the third year of licensure, and must complete a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless the applicant has at least three years of licensed teaching experience outside North Carolina. This applicant's 3 years out of state would appear to satisfy that exemption, but the passages do not confirm how it is documented.

The exam requirements for Special Education: General Curriculum (code 88091) are the Praxis Foundational Knowledge Test 5355 with a score of 145, or the Pearson Test 890 Foundations of Reading (233) plus the math requirement. Adapted Curriculum requires Praxis 5547 (156) and 5511 (148).

A permit to teach is not an appropriate route for this applicant, because a permit requires that the applicant has never been issued any other NC professional educator license, and the permit cannot be extended or renewed.

question: Teacher has a CPL in biology and an NC Emergency License in chemistry. Can they hold both and teach chemistry?

answer.summary: The passages do not say whether a CPL and an emergency license can be held at the same time, so that question is not covered. The durable route to teaching chemistry is adding chemistry to the CPL under LICN-013, by passing Praxis 5246 with a score of 146 or completing 24 credit hours with a C or better; the emergency license is valid only through June 30 of the fiscal year requested and cannot be renewed.

claims.text: An applicant may request to add a new license area to an existing IPL or CPL. To qualify for an additional teaching area, the applicant must either satisfy the licensure examination requirements for that area, or complete 24 credit hours of higher-education coursework in that area with a grade of C or better in each course.
The required chemistry licensure test is Praxis 5246, with a required score of 146.

An emergency license may be requested only if the applicant holds at least a bachelor's degree that includes at least 18 credit hours of coursework relevant to the licensure area, has not completed a recognized educator preparation program in that area, and does not qualify for a residency license.

Chemistry is a secondary license area listed under LICN-010 as a teaching classification, so it is a recognized teaching area for either a CPL add-on or an emergency license.

question: media coordinator with an MLS, no teaching experience, wants NC media license. Options?
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

answer.summary: A media coordinator license is a student services personnel license that requires completing an educator preparation program at the master's level or higher, plus passing the Praxis 5312 exam (score 154). Whether the MLS qualifies depends on whether it was completed through a recognized EPP and whether the candidate holds an out-of-state clear license, and the analyst needs to confirm those facts before the most likely path (an initial professional license) can be confirmed.

claims.text: Media Coordinator is one of the student services personnel license classifications.

To qualify for a student services personnel license, an applicant must have completed an educator preparation program at the master's (M), specialist (S), or doctoral (D) level. An MLS would meet the degree level only if it was completed through an EPP.

question: What's the difference between a Residency License and an Initial Professional License?

answer.summary: An Initial Professional License (IPL) is a three-year nonrenewable license for applicants who meet EPP or out-of-state qualifications, and it lets the holder practice as an independent professional educator. To qualify for an IPL, an applicant must either have completed a recognized NC educator preparation program (EPP) and be recommended by it, have completed an out-of-state EPP, or hold a clear out-of-state license and have fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in that jurisdiction.

A public school unit may request an IPL for an applicant under its employment who has completed all EPP requirements but has not yet satisfied the licensure exam requirements; in that case the EPP recommendation is not required.

A public school unit's governing body may request a Residency License for an applicant under its employment who meets G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) and has either completed at least 24 hours of coursework in the content area or passed the applicable licensure examination requirements.

To renew a Residency License, the employing school unit must document that the applicant is enrolled in a recognized EPP, is employed as a teacher in that unit, acquired at least six months of teaching experience in the preceding school year, and completed 10 days of professional development in the first year.

To convert a Residency License to an IPL or CPL, the applicant must meet the IPL or CPL requirements and be recommended by the EPP that prepared the licensee. If this is done by June 30 of the third year of the residency license, the IPL or CPL takes effect July 1 of the next fiscal year; otherwise the residency license expires and the IPL or CPL takes effect when the requirements are met.

A public school unit employing a teacher on a Residency License must provide at least three hours of field experience before the teacher begins teaching in the classroom and at least 10 hours over the first year.
A person who holds or previously held a Residency License is not eligible for a permit to teach or an emergency license in the same license area.
